title: EE-6204 Quiz 1 - Mock Paper 2 (graphical, simplex, sensitivity)
description: Second self-marking MCQ mock for EE-6204 Quiz 1. In scope only: the graphical method, the simplex method, and sensitivity analysis for the simplex method (per quizzes/quiz-1-official-announcement.pdf). Every item is agent-generated on fresh linear programs; no number needs a calculator. Not a prediction - see assessment/evidence-report.md. This template shows no countdown timer; sit it in 45-50 min on your own clock.

questions.prompt:
Spine LP (used in Parts A, B and C):

    maximize   z = 6 x1 + 5 x2
    subject to     x1 +   x2 <= 6        (resource R1)
                 3 x1 + 2 x2 <= 15       (resource R2)
                   x1 , x2 >= 0

Solve it by the graphical method. Enter the optimal objective value z.
For the spine LP (maximize 6 x1 + 5 x2 s.t. x1 + x2 <= 6, 3 x1 + 2 x2 <= 15, x >= 0), the optimal vertex (x1, x2) is:
questions.explanation: (3,3) gives z = 33, higher than (5,0) -> 30 and (0,6) -> 30. (4,2) is infeasible: x1 + x2 = 6 is fine, but 3(4) + 2(2) = 16 > 15 violates R2 - the trap is checking only one constraint. The maximum of a linear objective is attained at a vertex; here that vertex is (3,3), the intersection of the two resource lines.

questions.prompt: At the optimal vertex of the spine LP, which constraints are binding (hold with equality)?

options.text: Only R1 (x1 + x2 <= 6)
Both R1 and R2
Neither - the optimum is interior

questions.explanation: At (3,3): x1 + x2 = 6 (tight) and 3(3) + 2(3) = 15 (tight). Both slacks are zero. The optimum sits at the intersection of the two resource lines, so both are binding.

questions.prompt: For the spine LP solved graphically, select EVERY statement that is true:

options.text: The feasible region is bounded.
(5, 0) is a vertex of the feasible region.
(0, 6) is the optimal vertex.
At the optimum the iso-profit line 6 x1 + 5 x2 = k touches the feasible region at exactly one point.

questions.explanation: (a) True: the region is a closed polygon with vertices (0,0), (5,0), (3,3), (0,6). (b) True: (5,0) is where x2 = 0 meets 3x1 + 2x2 = 15, and x1 + x2 = 5 <= 6 there. (c) False: z at (0,6) is 30, less than 33 at (3,3). (d) True: the optimum is a unique vertex, so the highest iso-profit line meets the region at just the point (3,3). Exact-set scoring: tick a, b, d and leave c unticked.

questions.prompt:
Spine LP, objective 6 x1 + 5 x2. Keep the x2 coefficient at 5. Rotating the iso-profit line, over what range of the x1 coefficient c1 does the optimal vertex stay at (3, 3)?

Hint: the two edges through (3,3) are x1 + x2 = 6 (slope -1) and 3 x1 + 2 x2 = 15 (slope -3/2). The iso-profit line c1 x1 + 5 x2 = k has slope -c1/5.

options.text: any c1 > 0

questions.explanation: (3,3) stays optimal while the iso-profit slope lies between the two edge slopes: -3/2 <= -c1/5 <= -1, i.e. 1 <= c1/5 <= 3/2, i.e. 5 <= c1 <= 7.5. Outside this the optimum jumps to a neighbouring vertex. This matches the c1 range you would get from the final simplex tableau - graphical and tableau sensitivity agree.

questions.prompt:
Solve by the graphical method:

    minimize   z = 2 x1 + 3 x2
    subject to     x1 +   x2 >= 4
                   x1 + 3 x2 >= 6
                   x1 , x2 >= 0

The optimal point and value are:

options.text: No finite minimum - the problem is unbounded

questions.explanation: The feasible region is unbounded upward, but for a minimization that is fine - the objective is bounded below. Its vertices are (0,4), (3,1), (6,0). z: 12, 9, 12. Minimum z = 9 at (3,1), the intersection of x1 + x2 = 4 and x1 + 3 x2 = 6 (subtract: 2 x2 = 2). The 'unbounded' option confuses an unbounded feasible region with an unbounded objective.

questions.prompt:
Solve by the graphical method:

    maximize   z = 3 x1 + x2
    subject to     x1 + x2 <= 4
                   x1      <= 2
                        x2 <= 2
                   x1 , x2 >= 0

The optimum is at (2, 2). This vertex is best described as:

options.text: An unbounded vertex
An infeasible vertex
An interior point of the feasible region
A degenerate vertex - more than two constraint lines pass through it

questions.explanation: At (2,2) three constraint lines are active at once: x1 + x2 = 4, x1 = 2, x2 = 2. In two dimensions a vertex needs only two active constraints, so a third makes it degenerate. The Week 3 exercise-class Q1/Q2 show the same thing (all three constraint lines through the optimum). z = 3(2) + 2 = 8, but the question is about the vertex type.

questions.prompt: The spine LP feasible region is defined by x1 + x2 <= 6, 3 x1 + 2 x2 <= 15, x1 >= 0, x2 >= 0. Which ADDED constraint would be redundant (it would not change the feasible region at all)?
questions.explanation: Every feasible point already has x1 + x2 <= 6 <= 10, so x1 + x2 <= 10 never cuts anything - redundant. The others all remove feasible points: x1 <= 4 cuts off (5,0); x2 <= 2 cuts off (3,3); 2 x1 + x2 <= 6 cuts off (3,3) too (2(3) + 3 = 9).

questions.prompt:
Solve by the graphical method:

    maximize   z = 4 x1 + 6 x2
    subject to   2 x1 + 3 x2 <= 12
                   x1        <= 5
                        x2   <= 3
                   x1 , x2 >= 0

Which statement is correct?

options.text: The LP has a unique optimum at (1.5, 3)
The objective is unbounded
The LP has infinitely many optimal solutions - a whole edge, every point of which gives z = 24
The LP has a unique optimum at (5, 2/3)

questions.explanation: 4 x1 + 6 x2 = 2(2 x1 + 3 x2) <= 2(12) = 24, reached at EVERY feasible point with 2 x1 + 3 x2 = 12. The iso-profit line is parallel to that binding edge. The edge runs from (1.5, 3) to (5, 2/3); both endpoints and everything between give z = 24. The two 'unique optimum' options each name one endpoint as if it were the only optimum.

questions.prompt: To apply the simplex method to the spine LP, put the constraint 3 x1 + 2 x2 <= 15 into standard (equality) form. The correct form is:

options.text: 3 x1 + 2 x2 + s2 = 15,  s2 free

questions.explanation: A <= constraint takes a non-negative SLACK variable representing unused resource. Option a is a surplus (for >= rows). Option c, a free slack, breaks the 'unused amount is non-negative' meaning. Option d adds an artificial variable, only needed when there is no ready starting basic variable (= and >= rows).

questions.prompt: Spine LP, initial tableau (bottom row is z - c^T x, so it starts as [ -6, -5, 0, 0 | 0 ]; basis s1, s2; RHS 6 and 15). Which variable enters the basis first, and why?

options.text: x2, because -5 is negative and x2 has the smaller coefficient
s1, because it has the largest RHS ratio
None - the tableau is already optimal
x1, because -6 is the most negative bottom-row entry

questions.explanation: With the z - c^T x row, a negative entry marks a variable that can still improve z. Any negative may enter; the standard pick is the most negative, -6, under x1. The 'already optimal' option is wrong because negative entries remain. Slacks do not 'enter' from an all-slack starting basis.

questions.prompt: Spine LP, first pivot: x1 is entering. The initial rows are  s1: [1, 1, 1, 0 | 6]  and  s2: [3, 2, 0, 1 | 15]. Which variable leaves, and by what test?

options.text: s2 leaves: minimum ratio test gives 15/3 = 5 < 6/1 = 6
s1 leaves: 6/1 = 6 is the larger ratio, so s1 goes first
s2 leaves: it has the larger objective-row coefficient
Neither - x1 can increase without bound

questions.explanation: Minimum-ratio test over rows with a positive entry in the x1 column: 6/1 = 6 and 15/3 = 5. The smallest non-negative ratio, 5, is the s2 row, so s2 leaves. Taking the larger ratio (option b) would drive s2 negative. Both entries are positive, so it is not unbounded.

questions.prompt: In that first pivot of the spine LP (x1 enters, s2 leaves), what is the pivot element?

options.text: The 1 in the s1 row, x1 column
The 3 in the s2 row, x1 column
The 15 in the s2 row, RHS column
The -6 in the z row, x1 column

questions.explanation: The pivot element sits at the intersection of the entering column (x1) and the leaving row (s2): the coefficient 3. You divide that row by 3 and use it to clear the rest of the x1 column. The pivot is never in the z row or the RHS column.

questions.prompt:
After the first pivot the spine LP tableau is

    basis |  x1    x2    s1     s2   | RHS
     s1   |   0   1/3    1    -1/3  |  1
     x1   |   1   2/3    0     1/3  |  5
     z    |   0   -1     0     2    | 30

What is the current basic feasible solution?
questions.explanation: Basic variables take their RHS values: s1 = 1, x1 = 5. Non-basic variables (x2, s2) are 0. z is the RHS of the objective row, 30. The (3,3), z = 33 option is the final answer two pivots later, not this tableau.

questions.prompt: Looking at that same tableau (z row [0, -1, 0, 2 | 30]), is it optimal? If not, what happens next?

options.text: Not optimal - x2 enters next (its z-row entry is -1)
Not optimal - s2 enters next (its z-row entry is 2)
Optimal - the objective value 30 cannot be improved
Not optimal - x1 re-enters to increase further

questions.explanation: A negative bottom-row entry (-1 under x2) means x2 can still improve z, so the tableau is not optimal and x2 enters. A positive entry (+2 under s2) is not an improvement direction. x1 is already basic, so it does not 're-enter'.

questions.prompt:
The spine LP simplex run finishes with this tableau:

    basis |  x1   x2   s1   s2  | RHS
     x2   |   0    1    3   -1  |  3
     x1   |   1    0   -2    1  |  3
     z    |   0    0    3    1  | 33

What is the exact rule that says this is optimal (so the method stops)?

options.text: Both decision variables x1 and x2 are basic
The RHS column has no negative entries
Every entry in the z row is >= 0 (no negative reduced cost remains)
The objective value (33) equals the sum of the RHS entries

questions.explanation: For a maximization written with the z - c^T x row, optimality is exactly: no negative entry in the bottom row. 'Both variables basic' and 'RHS non-negative' are true of this tableau but neither is the stopping rule; the 'sum of RHS' statement is a coincidence, not a criterion.

questions.prompt:
A DIFFERENT maximization problem produces this tableau (bottom row is z - c^T x; basis x1, s1):

    basis |  x1   x2   s1   s2  | RHS
     x1   |   1   -1    0    1  |  5
     s1   |   0   -3    1    2  |  8
     z    |   0   -2    0    3  | 40

The z row still has -2 under x2. What do you conclude?

options.text: The tableau is optimal - a negative in the z row is acceptable once RHS is positive
The LP is unbounded: x2 would enter, but its column (-1, -3) has no positive entry, so the ratio test has no eligible row
x2 leaves the basis on the next step
Pivot on the -3 in the s1 row

questions.explanation: x2 has a negative reduced cost so it should enter, but every entry in its column is <= 0. Increasing x2 never forces a basic variable to zero, so z rises without bound: the LP is unbounded. You cannot pivot on a non-positive entry, and x2 is non-basic so it cannot 'leave'.

questions.prompt:
Another maximization run (bottom row z - c^T x) ends with this z row, basis (x1, s2):

    columns:  x1   x2   s1   s2  | RHS
    z row:     0    0    4    0  | 48

Every entry is >= 0, so the tableau is optimal. What does the 0 in the x2 column tell you?

options.text: The solution is degenerate
Nothing special - zeros in the z row are always normal
x2 = 0 is simply the value of a basic variable
x2 is non-basic with reduced cost 0, so it can enter without changing z: the LP has multiple optimal solutions

questions.explanation: The basis is (x1, s2), so x2 is non-basic. A non-basic variable with a 0 reduced cost can be pivoted in without changing the objective, giving a second optimal vertex and a whole optimal edge - alternative optima. Degeneracy is a BASIC variable equal to 0, a different thing. The 0 under s2 is unremarkable because s2 is basic; the 0 under non-basic x2 is the meaningful one.

questions.prompt: Suppose a >= requirement, 2 x1 + x2 >= 8, were added to a problem. To begin the simplex method with a ready identity starting basis, this row is written as:

options.text: 2 x1 + x2 - e3 + a3 = 8,  with e3 >= 0 (surplus) and a3 >= 0 (artificial)

questions.explanation: A >= row needs a surplus e3 to reach equality, and then an artificial a3 to serve as the initial basic variable (later driven to 0 by Big-M or two-phase). Option b is the <= rule. Option c has no non-negative basic variable to start from (-e3 cannot be basic at a feasible point). Option d makes the RHS negative, which the method disallows.

questions.prompt:
Spine LP final tableau:

    basis |  x1   x2   s1   s2  | RHS
     x2   |   0    1    3   -1  |  3
     x1   |   1    0   -2    1  |  3
     z    |   0    0    3    1  | 33

Enter the shadow price (dual value) of resource R1, the x1 + x2 <= 6 constraint.

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

questions.explanation: The shadow price of constraint i is the final z-row coefficient under its slack si. Under s1 the entry is 3, so one extra unit of R1 raises optimal z by 3 (within the allowable RHS range). Under s2 it is 1 - that is R2's shadow price, a common wrong pick.

questions.prompt: Resource R2 (3 x1 + 2 x2 <= 15) is fully used at the optimum. A supplier offers extra units of R2. Up to what unit price is buying more worth it, and with what caveat?

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

options.text: Up to 5 per unit (the objective coefficient of x1)
0 - extra units of a fully-used resource never help
Up to 1 per unit (the shadow price), and only while the total b2 stays inside its allowable range
Any price - a binding constraint is always worth relaxing

questions.explanation: The shadow price of R2 is 1 (the z-row coefficient under s2), so an extra unit adds 1 to optimal z - buying is worth it only if the marginal cost is below 1. And that rate holds only over R2's allowable RHS range; past it the basis changes and the price changes.

questions.prompt: In the spine LP, the right-hand side of R1 (x1 + x2 <= 6) increases to 7. Using the final tableau, the new optimal objective value is:

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

questions.explanation: Change = +1, and R1's shadow price is 3, so z goes from 33 to 33 + 3(1) = 36. Check the basis still holds: new basic values are x2 = 3 + 3(1) = 6, x1 = 3 - 2(1) = 1, both >= 0, so the shadow price is valid here. '33' ignores the change; 39 and 42 use the wrong rate.

questions.prompt:
Over what range of b2 (the R2 right-hand side, currently 15) does R2's shadow price stay equal to 1?

Final tableau s2 column: x2 row -1, x1 row +1.

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

options.text: b2 >= 0, always

questions.explanation: Perturb b2 by D. New basic values = old + D x (s2 column): x2 = 3 - D >= 0 gives D <= 3; x1 = 3 + D >= 0 gives D >= -3. So D in [-3, 3] and b2 in [15 - 3, 15 + 3] = [12, 18]. Inside this range the basis is unchanged and each unit of R2 is worth 1.

questions.prompt: A manager writes: 'R2's shadow price is 1, so at b2 = 25 the optimal z is 33 + 1 x (25 - 15) = 43.' Is this correct?

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

options.text: Yes - the shadow price of R2 is 1, so every extra unit adds exactly 1
No - the correct rate is 3, giving z = 63
Yes, provided b1 is unchanged
No - b2 = 25 is outside the allowable range [12, 18]; beyond it the optimal basis changes and z must be re-solved, so 43 is not reliable

questions.explanation: A shadow price is a LOCAL rate. It is valid only inside the RHS range (here [12, 18]). At b2 = 25 a basic variable would have gone negative long before, forcing a different basis with a different (smaller) marginal value, so linear extrapolation to 43 overstates z. This is the classic sensitivity trap.

questions.prompt: A proposed product 3 would earn 7 per unit and consume 1 unit of R1 and 2 units of R2 per unit made. Using the current shadow prices (R1: 3, R2: 1), should product 3 be introduced?

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

options.text: Yes - 7 exceeds 3(1) + 1(2) = 5, so product 3's reduced cost is +2 and making it raises z
No - 7 is far below the current optimal objective of 33
No - both resources are fully used, so there is no room for a new product
Cannot tell without re-running the simplex method from scratch

questions.explanation: Price the new column against the shadow prices: imputed resource cost = 3(1) + 1(2) = 5. Since the profit 7 > 5, the reduced cost is 7 - 5 = +2 > 0, so bringing product 3 in improves z - the current basis is no longer optimal for the extended problem. The 'no room' option is the trap: you would substitute production, not just add it.

questions.prompt:
The objective coefficient of x2 is currently 5. Over what range of that coefficient does the optimal basis (vertex (3, 3)) stay unchanged?

Final x2 row: [0, 1, 3, -1 | 3]. Add (change) x (x2 row) to the z row and keep it >= 0.

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

options.text: exactly 5 - any change moves the optimum

questions.explanation: Let c2 = 5 + d. Since x2 is basic, add d x (x2 row) to the z row: s1 entry 3 + 3d >= 0 gives d >= -1; s2 entry 1 - d >= 0 gives d <= 1. So d in [-1, 1] and c2 in [4, 6]. Within this range x* = (3, 3) is unchanged; only z = 33 + 3d moves.

questions.prompt: At the spine LP optimum, x1 = x2 = 3 and both constraints are binding (s1 = s2 = 0). Select EVERY statement that duality / complementary slackness makes true:

locators: method: sensitivity analysis for the simplex method

options.text: Because R1 is binding (s1 = 0), R1's shadow price is allowed to be positive.
Because both constraints are binding, both shadow prices must equal 0.
Because x1 > 0 at the optimum, the first dual constraint (w1 + 3 w2 >= 6) holds with equality.
The optimal dual values are w1 = 3, w2 = 1.

questions.explanation: Complementary slackness: a slack > 0 forces its dual value to 0, but a binding constraint (slack = 0) allows a positive dual value - so 'R1 binding allows a positive shadow price' is true and 'both binding means both prices 0' is false (it has the logic backwards). A decision variable > 0 forces its dual constraint tight - the x1 statement is true. The optimal dual values equal the shadow prices read from the z row, w = (3, 1); check b^T w = 6(3) + 15(1) = 33 = primal optimum. Tick a, c, d and leave b unticked.
